novel.justification: Binary covariates are this note's deliberate finite-alphabet specialization. Kim, Kennedy, and Naimi allow \(\mathbb R^d\)-valued covariates, so their paper is not a source for this binary-support condition.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Correct the source annotation without changing the support condition: Kim, Kennedy, and Naimi use \(\mathbb R^d\)-valued covariates rather than assuming binary covariates.

proposed.comparator_claim: Theorem 5.1 gives fixed-horizon nuisance-rate inference, while Theorem 6.1 compares incremental and deterministic inverse-weighting variances under a common constant propensity. The paired lower-bound construction is outside the common-positive-\(p\) class of Theorem 6.1 and therefore does not establish a minimax converse for that special class; identification and upper/stability statements may still specialize to it.
The paper derives and attains local efficiency bounds for behavior-dependent tilting and modified-treatment policies under Markov or non-Markov policy models.
The paper proves sharp finite-sample known-versus-unknown behavior-policy bounds for one-stage fixed-target bandit evaluation and uses Chebyshev approximation in a low-exploration regime.
Theorems 2 and 4 derive high-dimensional discrete-covariate lower bounds for one-time treatment-specific and homogeneous-effect functionals using moment matching and collisions.
Theorem 2 lower-bounds estimation error for a continuous-exposure static exponential-tilt estimand as the tilt grows.
The paper derives efficiency, minimax, and finite-tilt normality results for a multivariate static exposure tilt with one conditional normalizer.
Theorem 2 gives a parametric fixed-policy bias-variance expansion showing that longer-history behavior estimation reduces asymptotic variance while increasing finite-sample bias.
CoinDICE constructs behavior-agnostic policy-value intervals from embedded Markov occupancy equations and proves asymptotic and nonasymptotic coverage statements.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Qualify the transfer claim for Kim--Kennedy--Naimi Theorem 6.1 while preserving every other comparator entry.

prose_updates.tldr: Longitudinal incremental interventions retain bounded oracle likelihood-ratio variance when the per-period log-odds shift is \(c/\sqrt T\), but this local stability need not control the global cost of learning an unrestricted exponentially branching propensity tree. The paper proves exact finite-tree identification, a dimension-free local efficiency bound, computable truncated-prefix upper envelopes and every-depth collision converses, and the matched long-history frontier \(R(n,T,c)\asymp\min\{1,n^{-1}+c^2\}\) and \(L(n,T,c)\asymp\min\{1,n^{-1/2}+c\}\) once \(T\geq2k_n\). The unresolved kernel is the factor-two logarithmic elbow: a compatible-prefix polynomial approximation, a nested-count variance theorem, and legal-subtree testing priors are still needed for matching all-sample functions and the complete consistency and oracle-penalty phase diagram.

project_justification.fill: The paper proves finite-tree identification, the dimension-free local gradient bound, computable finite-history upper envelopes and collision-based converses, and the matched long-history frontier. Constructing and analyzing the occupancy-adaptive polynomial or factorial estimator, calibrating its honest connected interval, producing a matching legal-subtree moment-mixing converse, and evaluating the full optimization across the factor-two logarithmic elbow remain future work.

sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: The analyst receives only \(n,T,c\), the alphabets, and the trajectories. The proved finite-history rule deterministically selects a truncation depth and uses empirical prefix tries; no true propensity kernel is supplied. Occupancy-adaptive polynomial or factorial corrections for closing the unresolved elbow remain a proposed program. The oracle benchmark additionally supplies \(\Pi(P)\).

prose_updates.related_work: Kim, Kennedy, and Naimi, \cite{KimKennedyNaimi2021}, Introduction, Theorems 3.1, 4.1, 5.1, and 6.1, and the concluding discussion, supply the writing model: long histories and positivity motivate incremental interventions, after which identification and fixed-horizon efficiency lead to a many-timepoint precision question. Their Theorem 6.1 assumes a common constant propensity for a variance ratio and does not optimize risk over unrestricted history trees. The paired lower-bound construction is outside the common-positive-\(p\) class of Theorem 6.1 and therefore does not establish a minimax converse for that special class; identification and upper/stability statements may still specialize to it. Kennedy, \cite{Kennedy2019JASA}, gives the underlying support-respecting binary incremental functional and fixed-horizon efficiency theory. Kallus and Uehara, \cite{KallusUehara2024NaturalPolicies}, Definitions 1--2, Theorems 2 and 8--11, Algorithm 1, and the proofs in Sections 7--8, show how behavior dependence adds a score term to the influence function; their global horizon conclusions rely on policy-model structure and do not imply finite-sample uniform estimation over all histories. Ma, Zhu, Jiao, and Wainwright, \cite{MaZhuJiaoWainwright2022}, Introduction, Theorems 1--3, the Chebyshev construction near equation (64), and its proof, provide the closest switching, low-count polynomial, and behavior-mixture machinery, but their target policy is fixed and arms are not nested. Jiao, Venkat, Han, and Weissman, \cite{JiaoVenkatHanWeissman2015}, Introduction, the smooth--nonsmooth estimator construction, Lemma 4, Theorems 2--4, and the approximation--moment lower-bound section, supply the factorial-moment lift that the prefix recursion must adapt. Zeng, Balakrishnan, Han, and Kennedy, \cite{ZengBalakrishnanHanKennedy2024Discrete}, Introduction, Theorems 2 and 4, their fuzzy-hypothesis proofs, and Discussion, show that unseen discrete contexts and within-cell collisions create causal minimax penalties; their one-time weighted means omit sequential parent-sum compatibility. Schindl, Shen, and Kennedy, \cite{SchindlShenKennedy2024}, Theorem 2 and its Le Cam proof, and Huang, Dong, Lin, and Antonelli, \cite{HuangDongLinAntonelli2026}, Theorem 4 and the efficiency appendix, establish tilt-sensitive static continuous-exposure theory; \(\mathrm{prop:static\text{-}nonreduction}\) shows why those single-normalizer results do not flatten the present target. Zhou, Hanna, Zhu, Yang, and Shi, \cite{ZhouHannaZhuYangShi2025}, Introduction, Theorem 2 and its projection proof, and the concluding discussion, characterize a parametric fixed-policy history-length bias-variance tradeoff rather than an unrestricted minimax frontier. Liu, Bacon, and Brunskill, \cite{LiuBaconBrunskill2020}, Theorem 1, conditional Monte Carlo derivation, and Discussion, motivate prefix conditioning but establish only sufficient variance comparisons. Cai and Low, \cite{CaiLow2004}, Theorem 1, Section 2 construction, and Discussion, provide the ordered-modulus logic for expected length; CoinDICE, \cite{DaiEtAl2020CoinDICE}, Theorems 1--3 and the interval optimization, instead depends on Markov occupancy equations absent here. Robins, Li, Tchetgen Tchetgen, and van der Vaart, \cite{RobinsLiTchetgenVanderVaart2016TR}, provide higher-order influence-function and degenerate-\(U\)-statistic machinery under complexity-reducing projections, whereas the unresolved step must build the projection from raw prefix occupancy.
prose_updates.honest_scope: Identification is given, and the binary completely observed experiment is deliberately narrower than the EAGeR dropout analysis. The finite-history envelope, long-history theorem, zero-shift reduction, oracle benchmark, and local-gradient bound are proved. The compatible-prefix approximation and the full matched phase diagram remain first-class open questions. No Markov, smoothness, sparsity, positive-propensity floor, or supplied nuisance kernel is introduced. At \(c=0\) the target and both optimal rates reduce exactly to ordinary bounded-mean estimation. The paired lower-bound construction is outside the common-positive-\(p\) class of Theorem 6.1 and therefore does not establish a minimax converse for that special class; identification and upper/stability statements may still specialize to it. The proposal does not turn its rates into a numerical sample-size prescription for richer covariates or dropout.
